subChunks.title: Animation with Framer Motion
subChunks.hookHtml: CSS transitions handle simple state changes. JavaScript animation libraries handle everything else: physics-based spring animations, coordinated sequences, gesture-driven interactions, and layout animations that reflow when items are added or removed. Framer Motion is the production standard for React animation — declarative, performant, and deeply integrated with React's component model.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The motion component

Every HTML element has a motion equivalent. Add animation props directly:

import { motion } from 'framer-motion';

// Simple fade in:
<motion.div
  initial={{ opacity: 0 }}
  animate={{ opacity: 1 }}
  transition={{ duration: 0.3 }}
>
  Content
</motion.div>

// Slide in from left:
<motion.div
  initial={{ x: -100, opacity: 0 }}
  animate={{ x: 0, opacity: 1 }}
  exit={{ x: 100, opacity: 0 }}
  transition={{ type: 'spring', stiffness: 300, damping: 30 }}
>
  Sliding content
</motion.div>

AnimatePresence — animate on unmount

React removes elements immediately. AnimatePresence holds them long enough to animate the exit prop:

import { AnimatePresence, motion } from 'framer-motion';

function Toast({ message, visible }) {
  return (
    <AnimatePresence>
      {visible && (
        <motion.div
          key="toast"
          initial={{ opacity: 0, y: -20 }}
          animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }}
          exit={{ opacity: 0, y: -20 }}
          transition={{ duration: 0.2 }}
          className="toast"
        >
          {message}
        </motion.div>
      )}
    </AnimatePresence>
  );
}

Layout animations

When items are added, removed, or reordered, layout prop automatically animates the position change:

// Items rearrange smoothly when the list changes:
{items.map(item => (
  <motion.li
    key={item.id}
    layout
    initial={{ opacity: 0, scale: 0.8 }}
    animate={{ opacity: 1, scale: 1 }}
    exit={{ opacity: 0, scale: 0.8 }}
  >
    {item.title}
  </motion.li>
))}

Variants — orchestrating related animations

const container = {
  hidden: { opacity: 0 },
  visible: {
    opacity: 1,
    transition: {
      staggerChildren: 0.1, // Each child animates 100ms after the previous
    },
  },
};

const item = {
  hidden: { opacity: 0, y: 20 },
  visible: { opacity: 1, y: 0 },
};

<motion.ul variants={container} initial="hidden" animate="visible">
  {quests.map(q => (
    <motion.li key={q.id} variants={item}>{q.title}</motion.li>
  ))}
</motion.ul>

Gesture animations

<motion.button
  whileHover={{ scale: 1.05 }}
  whileTap={{ scale: 0.95 }}
  transition={{ type: 'spring', stiffness: 400 }}
>
  Accept Quest
</motion.button>

Vex: "Animation is communication. A toast that fades in says 'new information arrived'. A card that springs on hover says 'this is interactive'. A list that reflows says 'this item moved, not disappeared and reappeared'. Use animation to give users spatial context — not to show off."

storyBeats.text: A quest card that snaps in and out. No transition. No feedback. Vex adds three props. The card now slides in smoothly, responds to hover, and fades out with an exit animation.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: motion.div replaces div. initial is where you start. animate is where you go. exit is where you go when unmounting. AnimatePresence holds the element until the exit animation completes. The layout prop handles items that move position when other items are added or removed.

storyBeats.speaker: Quest card with enter/exit animation

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build an animated quest board:

  • Render a list of quests using motion.li with layout prop
  • Use AnimatePresence so removed quests animate out with exit={{ opacity: 0, x: -100 }}
  • Use variants with staggerChildren so quests animate in one after another on mount
  • Add whileHover={{ scale: 1.02 }} and whileTap={{ scale: 0.98 }} to quest items
  • A 'Add Quest' button adds a new item to the top
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a draggable quest card system using Framer Motion's drag prop. Cards can be dragged freely. When dropped, if the card is over a 'Completed' zone (a div in the lower half of the screen), it moves to the completed list. If dropped elsewhere, it snaps back. Use useMotionValue and useTransform to rotate the card slightly as it's dragged. Add a physics spring for the snap-back.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the role of AnimatePresence in Framer Motion. Why is it needed for exit animations? Walk through the variants system and why staggerChildren is powerful for list animations. Then explain the layout prop — what problem does it solve that CSS transitions can't?

questions.prompt: Why does Framer Motion require `AnimatePresence` for exit animations?
options: React removes elements from the DOM immediately when they're unmounted — AnimatePresence holds them in the DOM until the exit animation completes
AnimatePresence provides a queue so animations don't overlap
Without AnimatePresence, the initial animation won't trigger
AnimatePresence manages the z-index of animating elements
questions.answer: React removes elements from the DOM immediately when they're unmounted — AnimatePresence holds them in the DOM until the exit animation completes
questions.explanation: When a conditional render removes an element, React removes it from the DOM in the same render. By the time an exit animation would run, the element is gone. AnimatePresence intercepts the removal, plays the exit animation, then removes the element. Without it, exit props are ignored.

questions.prompt: What does the `layout` prop on a `motion` element do?
options: Automatically animates the element's position when it changes due to DOM reflow (e.g., another item being added or removed)
Locks the element's size and position during animation
Applies flexbox layout to the element's children
questions.answer: Automatically animates the element's position when it changes due to DOM reflow (e.g., another item being added or removed)
questions.explanation: When items are added to or removed from a list, remaining items shift position. Without layout, they jump immediately. With layout, Framer Motion records the element's position before the update, lets React reflow, then smoothly animates from the old position to the new one. This is called a FLIP (First, Last, Invert, Play) animation.

questions.prompt: What does `staggerChildren: 0.1` in a container variant do?
options: Each child element's animation starts 100ms after the previous child's animation starts, creating a cascading effect
Children animate 10% faster than the parent
The container waits 100ms before starting any children animations
Children animations are batched and run simultaneously after 100ms
questions.answer: Each child element's animation starts 100ms after the previous child's animation starts, creating a cascading effect
questions.explanation: staggerChildren delays the start of each child's animation relative to the previous child. With staggerChildren: 0.1 and 5 items: item 1 starts at 0ms, item 2 at 100ms, item 3 at 200ms, etc. The parent propagates its variant state (hidden/visible) to children, and children automatically pick up their own variant definitions.

questions.prompt: When should you use CSS transitions instead of Framer Motion?
options: For simple, state-driven style changes (hover, focus, active states) where physics-based or sequenced animation isn't needed
Always — CSS transitions are always more performant
Only for color transitions — Framer Motion handles transforms better
When the animation must work in older browsers that don't support Framer Motion
questions.answer: For simple, state-driven style changes (hover, focus, active states) where physics-based or sequenced animation isn't needed
questions.explanation: CSS transitions are zero-JS overhead for simple effects: button hover states, focus rings, color transitions. Reach for Framer Motion when you need: exit animations, physics-based springs, gesture-driven animation, coordinated sequences (variants, stagger), or layout animations that respond to DOM reflow. Matching the tool to the complexity keeps your bundle lean.
